name: Esther Evans

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Esther, thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group, with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm at the yard by half six, loading the van with my nail gun, the chop saw and my old Stanley planes, which nobody else is allowed to touch. Right now we're on the Millbrook housing estate, forty council flats for rent, and I run the second-fix carpentry: doors, skirting, stair balustrades, kitchen carcasses. I love the moment a staircase goes in and the place suddenly feels like a home. What wears me out is my knees on the stairs, and the subcontractor paying us under the going rate because they know there's nowhere else to go round here.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How long have you been doing this, and who's at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Thirty-nine years, since I was nineteen and the only girl on my apprenticeship course. My partner Glen is a caretaker at the primary school on Station Road, and our two lads are grown and gone, one's a bus driver and one's in the army. We've never had much put by. There's maybe three weeks of bills in the bank at any time, and the van's on finance, so the pension at sixty-six is what I'm counting the days to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now I'll read you five pictures of the future, one at a time. The first is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I've always said in the canteen: told you so. Every few years somebody comes on site with a gadget that's going to change everything, and we're still hanging doors by hand. Online I'd probably share something about the money that got wasted on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means I get to finish. Seven and a half more years of Millbrook-type jobs, my knees permitting, and then the pension. It doesn't fix the pay, mind, it just means the same old fight about the pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different. I'd keep going on the estate, keep pushing at branch meetings for the subbies to pay the proper rate, and try to keep a bit aside each month, though that never lasts past the van service. Maybe I'd finally get the knee looked at instead of putting it off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved, mostly. Like hearing the rain's stopped before you've got the roof on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the pay fight carries on either way. What's the fight right now, specifically?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The subcontractor pays us about two pounds an hour under what the agreement says, and they get away with it because the next firm is forty miles off. I've got the union rep coming out in January. I've been doing this so long I can tell you which foremen will sign a petition and which ones go quiet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on the Millbrook crew would you be thinking of in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kayla, my apprentice. She's twenty and she's quick, quicker than I was. In this picture she gets a full career like I had, and that's the bit that'd make me happy.

S0.say: I'd tell the canteen I told them so: every few years someone brings a gadget on site, and we're still hanging doors by hand. Online I'd point at the money wasted on the hype.
S0.think: Privately it means she gets to finish her last seven and a half years and reach the pension. It doesn't fix the low pay, it just leaves the usual fight about the pay.
S0.do: Keeps working second-fix on the Millbrook estate and pushes the union to make the subcontractor pay the agreed rate, with a rep due in January. Tries to put a little aside each month and finally gets her knee seen to.
S0.feel: Relieved, like the rain stopping before the roof is on, with the old worry about pay still there.
S0.quote: Like hearing the rain's stopped before you've got the roof on.
S0.fieldNote: Her first reflex is vindication; she has heard tech promises on site for decades. Her real stress is not AI but the subcontractor paying under the agreed rate, and she frames that as a union fight. She lights up talking about her apprentice Kayla.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At the branch I'd say this is exactly why we need the union stronger, not weaker. If the tasks are getting carved up, workers should have a say in how. I'd want something in the agreement about who gets retrained and on whose time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It worries me more than I'd let on. I don't use any of this stuff, I don't even have the app the site manager keeps on about. If the firm starts using machines to cut and set out the kitchens, I'm the one who looks slow and old, even if my joints are tighter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the union for a training course paid by the firm, not by me, because I can't afford a week without pay. I'd stay on second-fix as long as they'll have me and dig my heels in on the hand-finished work, the balustrades and the bespoke bits. And I'd cut back, the Friday fish and chips and the holiday caravan, to get a few hundred pounds aside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like when the new site manager walks the floor with a clipboard and doesn't say hello.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd want training on the firm's time. What if they said no?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd go to the branch and we'd make it a fuss, because the council is the client and the council can put it in the contract. Public money building public houses should come with decent terms. That's the one lever we've actually got.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first, money-wise?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The caravan week in Wales, which kills me because it's the only time Glen and I actually sit down. Then the Friday fish and chips. The van payment can't go, because no van, no work.

S1.say: She'd tell the branch this is why the union must get stronger, so workers decide how tasks get carved up. She wants retraining written into the agreement, paid by the firm.
S1.think: Privately she worries she'll look slow and old next to machines, because she never uses apps or AI. Her skill might not count for much if the firm values speed.
S1.do: Asks the union to win firm-paid training and pushes the council, as client, to write it into contracts. Holds on to hand-finished work like balustrades, and cuts the caravan week and the Friday takeaway to save a few hundred pounds.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like a new manager walking the floor with a clipboard and no hello.
S1.quote: Public money building public houses should come with decent terms. That's the one lever we've actually got.
S1.fieldNote: She sees collective bargaining and the public client as her only levers. Her private fear is being seen as slow, which she would never admit at the branch. She will not pay for retraining herself because she simply can't lose a week's wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be shouting about it, honestly. Online, on the picket, wherever. I'd be saying the government let tech companies do this to working people without a plan, and they need to stop it or pay for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record? It means I'm finished at fifty-eight with three weeks of money in the bank and eight years to the pension. Nobody's hiring a woman my age to do anything, and I've never touched a computer for work. I don't know how we'd pay the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, I'd find out what the pension rules are for going early, and whether there's any hardship scheme. I'd join every protest the union called. Glen's job might hold a bit longer than mine, so we'd live on his wage and cut everything else, and I'd ask the lads if they could help, which I'd hate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick. Like a scaffold going out from under you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've got about two years' warning in this one. Does that time help at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really, because two years isn't long enough to save anything on what I earn. It's just two years of watching it come. Maybe I'd work every hour going in those two years, weekends, any private job, to put a bit aside, but my knees won't take a lot of that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your sons when you asked them for help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably say it as a joke first, "your mum's been made redundant by a toaster." Then I'd cry in the van after. I spent their whole childhood telling them work is how you stand on your own feet.

S2.say: She'd shout about it everywhere, saying the government let tech firms do this to working people with no plan. She'd demand it be stopped or paid for.
S2.think: Privately she sees herself finished at 58 with three weeks of savings and eight years to the pension. She doesn't believe anyone would hire her and doesn't know how they'd pay the rent.
S2.do: Checks early pension rules and any hardship scheme straight away, and joins every union protest. Lives on Glen's wage, cuts everything else, takes any weekend work her knees allow in the two years, and asks her sons for help.
S2.feel: Sick and frightened, like a scaffold giving way, with shame at needing help from her sons.
S2.quote: I'd probably say it as a joke first, "your mum's been made redundant by a toaster." Then I'd cry in the van after.
S2.fieldNote: The two years of warning does nothing for her, because her pay leaves no room to save. Her deepest hurt is the idea of asking her sons for help after teaching them self-reliance. Anger at government and tech firms is real, but under it she sounds out of options.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before, I'd be loud, but I'd also be at the branch saying we've got five years, so let's use them. Get a deal now: protected wages for older workers, or a bridge to the pension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's still bad, but five years puts me at sixty-three. That's close enough to the pension that a bridge might actually be possible. It's the difference between drowning and treading water.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push hard for a pension bridge in the union's demands and write to our MP. I'd try to clear the van finance in those years so that's one bill gone. I wouldn't retrain, I'm not going to become something else at sixty, but I'd make myself the person they keep for the fiddly finishing until the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still scared, but there's a plan in it, and a plan helps me sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra time between two years and five actually change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Clearing the van, mostly, that's about three years of payments left. And Kayla gets five years to get her ticket and find her feet somewhere, maybe in maintenance or repairs. And I get to fight for something instead of just fighting against it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you won't retrain. Is that a choice or a feeling?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bit of both, if I'm honest. I don't want to sit in a classroom with people my sons' age learning something that might be gone too. But I also know I've never been good with screens, and I'm not going to pretend otherwise to you.

S3.say: She'd still be loud but would tell the branch to use the five years to win a deal, such as protected wages or a bridge to the pension for older workers.
S3.think: Privately five years takes her to 63, close enough for a pension bridge to be possible. She calls it the difference between drowning and treading water.
S3.do: Campaigns for a pension bridge through the union and writes to her MP. Pays off the van finance over the next three years and holds on as the person kept for fiddly finishing work, without retraining.
S3.feel: Still scared, but having a plan lets her sleep.
S3.quote: It's the difference between drowning and treading water.
S3.fieldNote: The extra three years matter mostly for one bill, the van, and for getting closer to pension age. She is frank that refusing to retrain is partly a choice and partly not trusting herself with screens. She keeps thinking of her apprentice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is enough time for a decent government to do it properly. No excuses. Retraining for the young ones, a proper pension for the old ones, and the companies who profit paying their share.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, really, I'd be sixty-eight by then, so I'd be out of it. Retired, if my knees get me there. It's Kayla and the lads I'd worry about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on on the estates, same as I'd planned. I'd keep up the union work, maybe take a bigger role in the branch because I'd have the time near the end. I'd tell Kayla to learn the side of it that the machines can't do yet, and I'd nag my youngest to think about life after the army.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly sad for the trade. A bit uneasy about the young ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be retired. What would you think, walking past a site run by robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stand there like one of those old men at the fence watching the diggers. I'd want to know who's checking the joints. I've seen what happens when a staircase is out by five millimetres, and I'd bet a robot would never get the feel for old timber.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would anything about how you live change before then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. We'd still be counting pennies. I suppose I'd stop dreaming about doing a bit of private joinery after I retire, because there'd be no call for it, and that was going to be our caravan money.

S4.say: She'd say a decade is plenty of time for a decent government to act, with retraining for the young, a proper pension for the old, and profiting firms paying their share.
S4.think: Privately she'd be 68 and retired by then, so the worry is for her apprentice and her sons rather than herself.
S4.do: Carries on with estate work as planned and takes a bigger role in her union branch near the end. Urges her apprentice to learn what machines can't do yet and nudges her younger son to plan for life after the army.
S4.feel: Sad for the trade and a little uneasy for the young ones.
S4.quote: I'd stand there like one of those old men at the fence watching the diggers. I'd want to know who's checking the joints.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years she is past retirement, and her concern shifts to the trade and the young. One quiet loss emerged: the private joinery she hoped would pay for holidays in retirement. Her doubt that machines could feel old timber is pride as much as prediction.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, no question. That's the one where I'm out with nothing and too young for the pension. What would help is a bridge, a payment from when the work goes to when the pension starts, and the firms that profit paying into it, not people like Glen through their taxes.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about the women. When I started, they told me I wouldn't last a year on site. I lasted thirty-nine. If the machines come, I'd like somebody to remember there were women like me who built half these estates.

headlineQuote: I spent their whole childhood telling them work is how you stand on your own feet.
portrait: Esther Evans is a 58-year-old second-fix carpenter and union stalwart who runs finishing work on a council housing estate, with three weeks of savings and a van on finance. She has never used AI and doesn't intend to start, and she sees the union and the public client as her only real levers. A plateau would let her reach her pension, while steady change makes her fear looking slow. AGI in two years leaves her panicked at the thought of losing work at 58 and asking her sons for help, but five years gives her room to fight for a pension bridge, and with ten years she would be retired and grieving mainly for the trade.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because she would be out of work with almost no savings and eight years short of her pension.
whatWouldHelp: A bridge payment from losing work until the pension starts, funded by the companies that profit rather than by ordinary taxpayers.
